config.title: Train Delay Compensation in Berlin - FAQ
config.subtitle: What a delayed train out of Berlin is worth, when your ticket stops being locked to it, what BVG owes you inside the city, and how to file the claim.

items.q: How much do I get if my train from Berlin is an hour late?
items.a: **25 percent of the fare you paid for that single journey**, measured by the delay at your destination station, not at departure. From 120 minutes it becomes **50 percent**. A 29.90 euro saver fare to Hamburg arriving 70 minutes late pays back **7.48 euros**; the same ticket 130 minutes late pays back **14.95 euros**.

items.q: Why did my delayed S-Bahn claim pay nothing?
items.a: **Because of the 4 euro floor.** Deutsche Bahn does not pay out compensation amounts under 4 euros, and 25 or even 50 percent of a single Berlin AB fare never reaches that. Inside the city the compensation rules exist on paper but the arithmetic cancels them, which is why a late U-Bahn or S-Bahn is worth walking away from and not worth a form.

items.q: My train is late. Can I just take a different one?
items.a: **Yes, from 20 minutes of expected delay at your destination.** Berlin day trips are usually booked on Sparpreis fares that are locked to one train, and that lock comes off at 20 minutes. You may continue on the same route or another one at no extra cost. Twenty minutes is a much lower bar than the compensation thresholds, so this is the rule that fires most often.

items.q: Can I cancel the trip and get my money back?
items.a: **From 60 minutes of expected delay, yes, in full.** You can abandon the journey and have the whole fare refunded. If you already travelled part of the route you can claim the unused part, and if the trip has become pointless you can claim the used part too. On a Berlin day trip that is often the better trade: take the refund and spend the day in the city instead.

items.q: What happens if I miss the last train back to Berlin?
items.a: **A taxi or bus is covered up to 120 euros.** The conditions are specific: a delay of 60 minutes or more or a cancellation, on the last scheduled connection of the day, where you can no longer reach the destination station by 24:00, and where the railway provides no replacement and cannot be reached on the spot. The same applies to arrivals between 00:00 and 05:00. If continuing the same day is impossible and no room is arranged for you, reasonable hotel costs are covered as well. **Keep every receipt.**

items.q: Does BVG pay compensation for a late U-Bahn, tram or bus?
items.a: **It sends a free ticket, not money.** BVG's customer guarantee applies from more than 20 minutes late through BVG's own fault. The useful part is the night clause: if it happens **between 23:00 and 05:00** and you have to take a taxi, BVG reimburses the fare **up to 25 euros**. The completed guarantee certificate has to reach BVG Kundendialog within **14 days**, which is a far tighter deadline than the railway's.

items.q: I have a Deutschlandticket. What do I get?
items.a: **Flat amounts, because there is no single-journey price to take a percentage of.** From 60 minutes at your destination, a regional travel card pays **1.50 euros** second class and 2.25 euros first class; a long-distance travel card pays **5 euros** second class and 7.50 euros first class, capped in total at **25 percent of the card's value**. On its own 1.50 euros sits under the 4 euro payout floor, so bundle several delays into one claim. Travel-card holders may count cases from 20 minutes upward when bundling.

items.q: When are they allowed to pay me nothing?
items.a: **Only for extraordinary circumstances outside railway operations**: extreme weather, a major natural disaster or a major public health crisis that the operator could neither foresee nor avoid. The bar is high, and an ordinary autumn storm or normal seasonal flooding does not clear it. Signal failures, staff shortages, broken trains, engineering overruns and strikes stay on the railway's side and still pay.

items.q: How and when do I file the claim?
items.a: **Get the delay confirmed while you are still in the station**, by having a Fahrgastrechte form stamped or by noting the train number with the scheduled and actual arrival times. Then file online through your DB account or the order lookup on bahn.de, in the DB Navigator app, at a DB Reisezentrum, or by post to DB Fernverkehr AG, Servicecenter Fahrgastrechte, 60647 Frankfurt am Main. The legal deadline is **three months** after the journey, although DB says it is still accepting claims up to twelve months as a transitional practice. **Ask for the bank transfer, not the voucher.**

items.q: Do regional trains that are not red count?
items.a: **Yes, the same passenger rights apply.** ODEG and other operators run a large share of the Brandenburg regional network out of Berlin, and a delay on one of their trains carries the same 60 and 120 minute thresholds. The only difference is the address: the claim goes to the operator that ran the train, not automatically to Deutsche Bahn.
